Mongolia is preparing for its first early presidential election after President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa resigned amid corruption allegations, having called for constitutional reform before leaving office.

Mongolia will hold a snap presidential election after President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa resigned amid corruption allegations.

Mongolia’s parliament, the State Great Khural, approved the president’s resignation on Thursday, with 96 of the 104 lawmakers present voting in favour of the motion, according to state news agency MONTSAME.

This marks the first time a sitting Mongolian president has resigned before completing their term.

On Tuesday, the 58-year-old president announced his resignation to allow him to prove his innocence in relation to corruption allegations. Khurelsukh denies any wrongdoing.

“I have never lied, stolen or deceived others,” Khurelsukh said at a press briefing on Tuesday, according to MONTSAME.

Khurelsukh has been accused by Nyambaatar Khishgee, former mayor of Ulaanbaatar and a member of a rival faction within the ruling Mongolian People’s Party (MPP), of taking $25 million (€23 million) in bribes.

The allegations concern a railway contract awarded to Bodi International, a Mongolian conglomerate, in 2019, when Khurelsukh was serving as prime minister.

The project involved the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway, which connects Mongolia’s coal-producing region to the border with China.

Bodi International has denied paying bribes to government officials.

Calls for constitutional reform

Before leaving office, Khurelsukh called for a constitutional referendum alongside the upcoming presidential election.

He suggested either introducing a bicameral parliament that would elect the president or shifting to a presidential system with greater executive powers.

Parliament has yet to announce a referendum on the proposed constitutional changes.

A new presidential election must be held within four months of the president’s resignation. Until a new president is elected and sworn into office, Parliamentary Speaker Byambatsogt Sandag is exercising presidential powers.

Parliament must announce the election date within 20 working days of the vacancy, and at least 70 days before the election.

Originally, the next presidential election was to be held in the summer of 2027. The winner of the early election will serve a single six-year term.

This means they will serve beyond Mongolia’s next two parliamentary elections, expected in 2028 and 2032 under the regular electoral cycle.

Political instability

Mongolia has experienced several high-profile political resignations in recent years.

In June 2025, former Prime Minister Luvsannamsrai Oyun-Erdene resigned after losing parliamentary support amid corruption allegations, which he denied.

In March 2026, Oyun-Erdene’s successor, Zandanshatar Gombojav, also resigned amid rising tensions within the ruling MPP and a parliamentary boycott by the opposition.

Relations with Europe

Mongolia has been seeking to improve relations with international partners other than its two powerful neighbours, China and Russia.

The country has long followed a foreign policy known as the ‘Third Neighbour Policy’, with the aim of improving relations with international partners, including the European Union.

Just one month before his resignation, Khurelsukh went on a state visit to Germany. During this visit, he met German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

As part of the visit, Mongolia and Germany signed a joint declaration to strengthen their existing strategic partnership. This includes cooperation on renewable energy, education and security.

In a statement following a meeting in Brussels on 29 June, the EU reaffirmed its support for Mongolia’s Third Neighbour Policy.

The EU described its partnership with Mongolia as based on democracy and the rule of law, while reaffirming its support for the country's economic diversification.

Euronews Hungary head Attila Kert has been tapped to run Hungary's public broadcaster, which faces an overhaul after years of bias criticism under Viktor Orbán. He pledges to restore credibility, launch streaming and probe Russian influence.

Euronews journalist Attila Kert has been selected as chief executive of Hungary's public broadcaster, Hungarian Radio and Television (MRTV).

Kert has led Euronews' Hungarian team in Budapest since 2013.

Under the previous government, led by Viktor Orbán, the national broadcaster was criticised by NGOs and the European Union for political bias. The institution now faces a reorganisation aimed at delivering objective, independent coverage and completing its digitalisation.

Twenty-seven candidates applied for the post, of whom 14 were found eligible. They set out their plans at a hearing earlier this week, ahead of the decision by the Independent Public Media Board, the body overseeing the transition.

"I am proud to have worked with Euronews for over 13 years. The experience I gained here has helped me a lot in my application for the new position. Without Euronews, I would be less. I am grateful to all my colleagues and thank them," Kert said.

In his presentation, Kert vowed to restore the broadcaster's credibility while reorganising it to become financially sustainable. His plans include setting up a streaming platform and investigating possible Russian influence.

Editorial Director of Euronews, Claus Strunz, said the decision is proof of the journalistic quality and editorial independence of Euronews in Hungary.

“Attila Kert believes in freedom of expression and the power of images and knows how to exercise both responsibly in every situation.

Over the past 13 years as head of our Hungarian service, he has played a pivotal role in safeguarding and strengthening Euronews’ independence and editorial neutrality, both internally and externally, in a highly polarised political and media environment.

His move from a renowned private media organisation to public-service broadcasting therefore marks a significant moment in the history of Hungarian media. Euronews is losing one of its finest journalists, while Hungarian public-service television is gaining in journalistic quality, stature and profile.

We also view his appointment to this important position as a testament to the journalistic quality and independence of Euronews in Hungary,” Strunz said.

Public broadcaster faces reorganisation

The Hungarian public broadcaster faced years of criticism under the Orbán government over bias and disinformation.

The Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) found that MRTV's coverage was systematically skewed, with news programmes "openly and disproportionately" supporting the ruling parties' narrative while marginalising or negatively portraying opposition voices.

After his landslide election victory in April, Péter Magyar vowed to shut down the organisation and create an independent, objective outlet.

In July, the broadcaster went off air for one day, replaced by an on-screen apology: "Public media cannot lie. We apologise because we did this anyway."

Before joining Euronews, Kert held several senior roles in Hungarian media. He was editor-in-chief of the commercial networks TV2 and ATV, and later head of news at the national broadcaster.

He was appointed to lead the Hungarian-language edition of Euronews in February 2013.

In 2026, the independent Italian media research institute Osservatorio di Pavia published an audit of Euronews Hungary's coverage of the election campaign. It scored the channel 99% for editorial independence and 98% for balanced coverage.

The fridge attacks were one of 16 incidents mapped by DigitalEurope, the trade association for Europe's digital technology industry, based in Brussels, Belgium, between 18 October and 18 November.

Eleven were cyberattacks. Hackers took an energy company's IT systems in Norway, closed a district hospital's emergency room in Germany and stole data from a tunnel builder working across Denmark and Germany.

At an unnamed EU institution, HR, payroll and medical systems were knocked offline. The personal data of 18 senior officials from Italy, Germany and the Netherlands was published, and espionage malware was found in Romanian government email.

About €100 million was taken from a French bank through one of its suppliers, more than 700 fintech customer accounts were exposed in Italy, and a Danish shipping group's legacy system was raided for data.

The other five incidents were physical, including two sabotage plots. About 80 aircraft lost GPS over the North Sea, drones forced Moldova to close its airspace, and hoax bomb threats hit more than 35 flights across Europe.

"Resilience is no longer just an IT department job," said Cecilia Bonefeld-Dahl, DigitalEurope's director general. "It is security policy and industrial policy."

The group says its list is not exhaustive. Ransomware gangs alone list dozens of European victims every month.

The password is 12345

The November wave was not the first. In mid-October, hackers took over refrigeration units in at least 350 supermarkets in France, including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché and Coopérative U stores, and manually overrode their temperatures.

France's cybersecurity agency said the units ran software from Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell systems. Danfoss said many had reached the end of their life, no longer received security updates or ran outdated firmware.

Supermarket refrigeration is often connected to the internet so contractors can monitor and repair it remotely. Security firm Forescout found nearly 13,000 refrigeration control services openly reachable online in 99 countries.

In November, attackers exploited weak security and known flaws in Danfoss's AK-SM system manager. Many systems still used factory-default logins such as "Supervisor" and "12345".

George Nott, technology editor at trade magazine The Grocer, said the attackers found exposed login pages and used vulnerabilities that had already been patched. In Sweden, the Coop chain said the equipment in its seven affected shops was connected over old 4G mobile networks.

Xavier Bellekens, chief executive of cybersecurity firm Lupovis, said routing the controllers through VPNs would largely have removed the risk.

Who did it?

Of DigitalEurope's 16 incidents, seven have no named culprit. Attackers claimed four themselves, investigators suspect an actor in two without formally naming it, and only three have been publicly attributed by a government or researchers.

"That is what makes hybrid attacks work: cheap, deniable and hard to pin on anyone," the group said.

The fridge attacks show how hard the question is. Lupovis said its decoy systems recorded more than 276 attempts by 91 threat actors to probe Danfoss controllers over 10 days, peaking on 26 October and stopping at the end of the month.

The 14% figure is the digital share of the EU's 2021–2025 spending, including its post-pandemic recovery fund, rather than of the budget now being negotiated. And as an industry lobby, DigitalEurope speaks for many of the companies that would sell Europe that technology.

A survey by more than 200 specialists found that Madeira's marine reserves are working – but some species are still in peril.

Madeira's waters sit at an ecological crossroads in the North-East Atlantic. Migrating whales, seabirds and turtles pass through, and the archipelago is home to cold-water corals and one of the world's rarest seals. Yet large stretches of the sea around the Portuguese islands have never been properly studied.

The Madeira Ocean Expedition, which ran throughout October, set out to fill those gaps. Its findings will feed into decisions on how to manage and expand Madeira's marine protected areas, as the region works towards protecting 30 per cent of its sea by 2030, with at least 10 per cent fully protected.

"We cannot protect without understanding how the biodiversity functions and works," says João Canning-Clode, director of the MARE-Madeira research centre.

A health check at sea: 500 dives in Madeira's ocean

Madeira's regional government organised the expedition with the Oceano Azul Foundation, National Geographic Pristine Seas, the regional research agency ARDITI and Oceanário de Lisboa. Teams worked from the historic tall ship Santa Maria Manuela and a fleet of smaller boats around Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas Islands.

"In an expedition like this, we want to take a snapshot about the health of the marine environment," says Emanuel Gonçalves, chief scientist at the Oceano Azul Foundation.

Scientists completed nearly 500 dives, lowered more than 300 baited cameras, filtered seawater for traces of DNA, mapped the shoreline with drones and sampled for microplastics.

With no research vessel of its own yet, MARE-Madeira also hired a fishing boat. "The fishermen could see for the first time live images of some of the biodiversity that they are actually fishing," Canning-Clode says. "On the other hand, the scientific community can see firsthand how difficult their life is."

Signs that Madeira's ocean protections work

Early results suggest Madeira's reserves are making a difference. Limpets – grazing sea snails harvested as a local delicacy – were bigger and more abundant inside protected areas, a sign that limits on collecting them are working, and the largest groupers were recorded there too.

"The good news is that we have the science to show us that when we fully protect the ocean, the ocean responds," Gonçalves says.

The Mediterranean monk seal is another case in point. Hunted for centuries, it had almost vanished from Madeira by the late 1980s, when only six to eight animals were thought to remain. The Desertas Islands became a nature reserve in 1990, partly to protect it. Today the species "is a beacon of hope", Gonçalves says. "The population is increasing in numbers. Now that increase is very slow because they are very slow breeders."

The expedition also achieved the first-ever satellite tagging of a Blainville's beaked whale in the North-East Atlantic. Early tracking data show the animal favouring waters south of the Desertas, close to the fully protected area.

But one finding stands out for the wrong reason. Fewer than 10 sharks were recorded across the entire expedition. The organisers call this scarcity concerning and in line with wider worries about sharks in the Atlantic.

Into the deep: The difficulties of exploring Madeira's ocean

By area, Madeira is mostly deep sea. "It's an ocean state, a deep ocean state," says Diva Amon, a marine scientist on the Oceano Azul Foundation's board. "And the deep sea is a very difficult place to study."

Drift cameras developed by researchers in the Azores and lowered from a fishing boat reached 1,060 metres. They revealed sponge fields and large black corals that may be several hundred years old – alongside lost fishing lines and a glass bottle.

Closer to the surface, the habitat-mapping team's highlight was a dense black coral garden off Porto Santo, known as Ariel's Garden after the team's pink underwater robot. "Our torpedo is pink, so by majority vote it's called Ariel, after the little mermaid from the Disney film," says João Monteiro, a researcher at MARE-Madeira and the University of Madeira.

A second expedition in 2027 will explore the deepest waters. Amon hopes it will reveal "places that are as iconic as the Grand Canyon or the Okavango Delta".

For Paul Rose, head of expeditions at National Geographic Pristine Seas, Madeira's location matters. "People think about ocean protection, they think about the Pacific... It all seems a bit remote," he says. "But if they see huge, beautiful, functioning, proven marine protected areas in Europe, it's closer to home."

Just over 10 per cent of the global ocean now lies within protected areas, according to IUCN and UNEP-WCMC – a third of the way to the 2030 goal. "We've really got to protect 30 per cent or we're in big trouble," Rose says.

Employers across Europe increasingly value skills while formal qualifications are still significant. Euronews Business takes a close look at which countries are most ready for a skills-first approach with experts explaining the gaps.

The labour market is constantly changing. New jobs are emerging and new skills are required. Degrees still matter in Europe’s job market, but employers are paying more attention to what people can actually do, experts say.

“The currency of the labour market is shifting from traditional credentials alone towards a stronger focus on skills,” OECD’s ‘A Skills‑First Labour Market’ report says.

This is known as a skills-first approach.

“In practice, skills-first hiring is not about replacing degrees altogether, but about giving greater weight to individuals’ demonstrated skills, wherever they were acquired, to improve the matching of talent to jobs,” Glenda Quintini, senior economist at OECD, told Euronews Business.

Dr Soon-Joo Gog, senior director at the Centre for Skills-First Practices at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, emphasised that skills-first does not mean skills only. It is an operating principle. Individuals and employers use demonstrated skills, alongside qualifications.

The OECD’s Skills-First Readiness and Adoption Index measures how ready each country is for this approach.

How does the index work?

The index gives each country a score between 0 and 1. A higher score means a country is better prepared for skills-first practices and uses them more widely.

The index looks at how well countries identify, develop, recognise and reward skills. This includes adult learning, the use of skills data, public support for training and how far employers value what workers can show they are able to do.

Sweden and France lead the way

Sweden has the highest score in Europe at 0.70, followed by France (0.69), the UK (0.65) and Belgium (0.64).

“Countries such as Sweden and France perform strongly overall, although there is no single pathway to building a skills-first labour market,” Quintini said.

“Sweden, for example, stands out for its strong enabling framework, including the use of skills intelligence data and public support for skills development.” she added. 

Finland (0.63), Czechia (0.61), Norway (0.61) and Latvia (0.61) also score above the European average.

The average across 23 European countries is 0.58. Spain (0.59), Denmark (0.58), Portugal (0.58), Italy (0.58), Lithuania (0.58), Poland (0.58) and Austria (0.58) are close to this average.

Germany (0.57), Switzerland (0.57) and the Netherlands (0.56) are slightly below it.

Hungary (0.45) and Greece (0.46) have the lowest scores. Turkey (0.52), Slovakia (0.54) and Slovenia (0.54) also score low.

Quintini noted that countries at the lower end of the index often face greater barriers related to adult learning participation and the development of broader learning ecosystems.

“The gap is therefore not simply about education systems, but it reflects how effectively countries identify, develop, recognise and reward skills in the labour market,” she said.

The US scores slightly above the European average at 0.60. Canada (0.55), Japan (0.51) and South Korea (0.48) are below it.

Gog pointed out that most European countries have laid the foundations but the harder step is to make these practices routine.

“That takes time and requires coordinated effort across the system,” she said.

Degrees still matter, but they are not the only signal

Experts agree that degrees remain important. But employers increasingly want to see skills as well.

“Degrees continue to matter in OECD labour markets, particularly because they remain a widely recognised signal of knowledge and capabilities,” Quintini said.

“However, employers are increasingly looking beyond formal qualifications and paying greater attention to the actual skills that workers possess and can demonstrate.”

She said skill shortages are driving this shift. Firms also need to find talent from a wider range of backgrounds, and skill needs are often changing faster than education systems can adapt.

As of 2025, more than 70% of employers across OECD countries report difficulties filling vacancies because of a lack of skilled talent. At the same time, around a third of workers say they are either over-skilled or under-skilled for their current job.

Significance of degrees varies by occupation

“Degrees still matter but their importance varies considerably by occupation and the real requirements are not always made transparent to jobseekers,” Pawel Adrjan, director of economic research at Indeed, told Euronews Business.

Indeed research found that only 14% of UK job postings explicitly mention formal education requirements, compared to 50% in the US.

He underlined that degrees remain important in specialist and highly regulated professions in practice.

“The key distinction is that a degree remains a valuable signal of knowledge and capability but it is not necessarily the only way candidates can demonstrate the skills required to do a job,” he added.

Skills need to evolve rapidly

Anna Toni, senior specialist at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment in Finland, emphasized that stakeholders increasingly recognise that valuable skills are acquired not only through formal education, but also through work experience, volunteering, hobbies and other life experiences. New tools and methods are being developed to identify and validate these skills.

“Labour markets are changing faster than before, driven by factors such as digitalisation, the green transition and AI. Skills need to evolve rapidly, and education and employment policies must adapt accordingly,” she told Euronews Business.

Skills or degrees: Which pays more?

The OECD found that on average, extra education raises wages by about 16%, while better numeracy skills raise them by about 9%, when comparing gaps of similar size.

This finding shows that employers still place substantial value on educational credentials as signals of productivity, especially when information on workers’ skills is limited according to Quintini.

In the OECD index, below 1 means education pays more than skills. France is the only European country above 1 at 1.33. This means a numeracy gap pays about a third more than an education gap of the same typical size.

“This [in France] may reflect a labour market and policy environment that is more conducive to recognising and valuing demonstrated skills,” she said.

Gog warned that the test covers numeracy only, so it misses the technical, social and job-specific skills that many jobs need.

Residents of Barnham back symbolic independence vote after government proposes accommodating around 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former RAF base.

A village in eastern England has voted overwhelmingly in favour of symbolically leaving the United Kingdom in protest against government plans to accommodate hundreds of asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.

Residents of Barnham, in Suffolk, voted 257 to 16 in favour of seeking a special status similar to that enjoyed by the Crown Dependencies of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man. One ballot was spoilt in Saturday’s vote, in which around 500 residents were eligible to take part.

The vote is purely symbolic and has no legal force. It does not mean Barnham can leave the United Kingdom or acquire Crown Dependency status. Any such change would require formal agreement and constitutional action by the UK authorities.

The former Royal Air Force site has been identified as a potential location for accommodating around 930 asylum seekers while their applications are processed. The government is seeking to move away from using hotels and towards accommodation at former military sites.

No final decision on RAF Barnham asylum plans

The government has stressed that no final decision has been made on whether RAF Barnham will be used to accommodate asylum seekers.

It said that, should the plans go ahead, it would work closely with local authorities and Suffolk Police to ensure the safety and security of the community.

The Home Office also cited the example of Wethersfield in Essex, where male asylum seekers have been accommodated since July 2023, saying there was “no evidence of rising crime in the area”.

A Home Office spokesperson said the government was pursuing a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country and had saved more than £1bn (approximately €1.19bn) in costs since the general election.

The plans include closing all asylum hotels and relocating people to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

The spokesperson added that the proposed facilities would be self-contained and equipped with round-the-clock security and CCTV to minimise the impact on surrounding communities.

Residents protest over lack of consultation

The proposal has prompted protests among residents, who say they were not adequately consulted about a development that could have a significant impact on their small community.

A similar vote took place in Piddington, Oxfordshire, in September, where residents also backed a symbolic move to leave the UK in protest against plans to accommodate more than 1,000 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.

Piddington’s symbolic vote failed to halt the plans, and the village is now preparing a legal fight after the government granted planning permission.

From beachfront resorts to skyscraper hotels overlooking the Arabian Gulf, Qatar is home to a growing portfolio of luxury properties.

When Qatar hosted the FIFA World Cup in 2022 it wasn’t just its sporting infrastructure that got an upgrade – but also its collection of hotels and resorts.

Now, Qatar’s luxury hotel portfolio has grown with five-star properties extending from the centre of the capital city Doha to the country’s islands and coastline.

For travellers seeking a high-end stay, the choice extends beyond location, with properties offering everything from private beaches and spas to fine dining and stunning views of the Arabian Gulf.

Looking for a five-star stay in Qatar? Here are some of the best luxury hotels and resorts to consider in Doha and Lusail.

The Chedi Katara Hotel & Resort

Opened in November 2022 in Katara Cultural Village, The Chedi has 91 rooms, suites, and villas with Mughal- and Ottoman-style interiors and sea views. Each of its 32 villas has a private garden and pool.

It features a private beach with water sports and two pools – a 60-metre-long infinity pool and a 35 metre family pool. Its Eastern-inspired spa includes a couples’ room and separate hammams for men and women.

Dining options include overwater restaurant La Marsa, which is reached by jetty.

Fairmont Doha

Fairmont Doha shares the landmark Katara Towers with its sister property, the Raffles Doha, in Lusail Marina. Both opened in November 2022 for FIFA World Cup guests and VIPs.

The hotel’s 362 rooms and suites take inspiration from sleek megayachts, while a 57-metre “crystal swirl” chandelier runs through the lobby.

For active travellers, there’s Fairmont Fit and a climbing wall. For a more relaxed stay, Fairmont Spa features nine treatment rooms and a traditional hammam. There is also a main outdoor pool, a 25-metre indoor lap pool and a private pool for Fairmont Gold guests.

The hotel offers five dining options, including Provok, a pan-Asian restaurant with sweeping rooftop views.

Four Seasons Hotel Doha

On the Corniche in West Bay, the Four Seasons Hotel Doha originally opened in April 2005. After a complete interior design overhaul by French designer Pierre-Yves Rochon, it reopened in 2020 with renovated guest rooms, suites, floors, lobby and dining outlets.

As well as 237 rooms and suites, the hotel has a private beach and five pools, including grotto pools and pools with slides. Its three-storey spa and wellness centre has 11 treatment rooms and a large hydrotherapy area with an ice room.

Nobu Doha, one of the hotel’s culinary highlights, is located on a private peninsula overlooking the Arabian Gulf and Doha skyline.

Four Seasons Resort & Residences at The Pearl-Qatar

Opened in November 2023 on The Pearl island, the second Four Seasons property in Qatar combines a beachfront resort with private accommodation. It has 161 guest rooms and 84 private residences.

The resort has a private beach and three pools, including a 25-metre indoor pool. Guests can also use the luxury Loulou spa, with aqua-thermal facilities, while younger guests have access to the Kids for All Seasons programme, with activities for children aged 4-12.

Dining options include Chicago Rare, a modern steakhouse with views of the Gulf and live jazz.

Mandarin Oriental, Doha

Mandarin Oriental, Doha opened in March 2019 in the heart of Msheireb Downtown, with the popular Souq Waqif just a short walk away.

It includes 117 rooms, 41 suites and 91 serviced apartments, offering views of Barahat Msheireb town square and the city landscape.

The hotel has two rooftop pools, including a 25-metre lap pool. Its spa offers a signature “Singing Sand Dunes” treatment inspired by the desert dunes in Qatar.

Dining facilities include Mosaic, which has nine open kitchens serving dishes inspired by the Silk Route.

Marsa Malaz Kempinski, The Pearl-Doha

Opened in December 2014 on its own private island at The Pearl, Marsa Malaz Kempinski blends palatial Arabian and European design across its 281 rooms and suites. It is also just a short walk from Qanat Quartier’s colourful buildings and canals.

Guests can take part in water sports from the private beach and jetty, while children have their own pool and the Titan Tikes playroom. The outdoor pool area also has a large whirlpool, while the Marsa Malaz Spa offers a private indoor pool.

Dining options include the Doha outpost of Harry's Dolce Vita, an Italian restaurant that serves classic dishes.

The Ned Doha

Located in the former Ministry of Interior building on Doha’s Corniche, The Ned Doha opened in 2022. Its 90 rooms and suites feature 1970s-inspired interiors, with balconies overlooking the Arabian Gulf or neighbouring Al Bidda Park.

​Ned's Club includes a health club with a spa, a traditional Moroccan hammam and a 30 metre heated outdoor pool, while the hotel's central atrium hosts live performances.

Millie’s Lounge, one of several restaurants and bars, has curved booths and views of Doha's skyline, while Electric Diner is styled as a 1950s American diner.

Raffles Doha

Raffles Doha opened in November 2022 in Lusail’s landmark Katara Towers, whose curved design is inspired by Qatar’s crossed swords.

The hotel has 132 suites, each with dedicated butler service. The hotel’s 55-metre outdoor pool has private cabanas, while Raffles Spa has five private spa suites, each with its own hammam, jacuzzi, outdoor pool and treatment space.

Dining includes ALBA, an Italian restaurant that earned one star in the 2026 Michelin Guide Doha.

The Ritz-Carlton, Doha

Set on its own private island between The Pearl and Lusail, The Ritz-Carlton Doha has been a mainstay in the hotel scene since 2001.

It has 374 rooms and suites, with a beach offering watersports and cabanas. The resort also has a 25-metre indoor pool and active guests can use the two indoor tennis courts and a squash court.

Families can explore the Ritz Kids garden, where children can learn about local flora and sustainable gardening.

Dining includes STK Doha, a modern steakhouse with skyline views that also hosts the 3D Le Petit Chef experience.

Rosewood Doha

Officially opened in January 2026, Rosewood Doha is just steps away from Lusail's marina and boardwalk. The hotel offers 155 rooms and suites, 162 apartments and 276 residences, with the Reef Suite offering a butler service.

Asaya, a wellness club open to members, hotel guests and residents, features anti-gravity heated loungers and a padel court, along with a 25-metre lap pool and a family pool with a dedicated children's area.

Koo Madame, inspired by Madame Wellington Koo, a former First Lady of the Republic of China, is one of eight dining destinations at the hotel. There’s also The Butterfly Room, a dedicated tea lounge.

The St. Regis Doha

Personal butler service is part of every stay at The St. Regis Doha, regardless of room category. The West Bay hotel has 335 rooms and suites, with views across the Arabian Gulf or The Pearl.

The hotel has a private beach that offers a range of water sports and an outdoor Olympic-sized pool, with private poolside cabanas that include their own plunge pools, kitchenette, and flat-screen TVs.

Dining includes steakhouse Astor Grill and Sarab Lounge, known for its English afternoon tea with live music.

Waldorf Astoria Doha Lusail

Opened for the 2022 FIFA World Cup, Waldorf Astoria Doha sits on a private beach in Lusail, with 429 rooms, suites and apartments.

There’s a waterpark and Aloha Surf Club, which has a dedicated surf pool. The resort also has three swimming pools, including one for families. Children and teenagers have their own clubs, while the three-storey ESPA Life Spa features a private indoor pool, thermal facilities and a hammam.

The hotel’s F&B options include SUSHISAMBA, which has a beach club with a private pool surrounded by cocoon-style cabanas.
